html:
The Witwatersrand Gold Rush began in 1886, when gold was found on the Witwatersrand, a ridge in the Boer South African Republic (the Transvaal). It led to the founding of Johannesburg, which within ten years was the largest town in southern Africa.

The ore was low grade but the reefs were huge and ran deep underground. Mining them needed heavy machinery and large capital, so a few big mining houses took over. Many were led by men who had made fortunes at the Kimberley diamond fields, such as Cecil Rhodes. The Johannesburg Stock Exchange opened in 1887 to raise money for them.

The mines ran on black migrant workers from across southern Africa, hired on fixed contracts, housed in closed compounds and paid far less than white miners. This system of migrant labour and pass controls later became a base for apartheid.

Gold also brought war. The Transvaal government of Paul Kruger refused the vote to the many foreign white miners, called Uitlanders. Tension grew into the Second Boer War of 1899 to 1902, which put the goldfields under British rule. Together with diamonds, gold turned South Africa into an industrial economy, a change often called the Mineral Revolution. For most of the 1900s South Africa was the world's largest gold producer.
